title.en: Odenkirk's Heresy: Sketch Comedy as the Purest Art
title.de: Odenkirks Ketzerei: Sketch-Comedy als reinste Kunst

excerpt.en: Bob Odenkirk argues that sculpting something into 'art' drifts away from real life — and that sketch comedy, disposable and unpolished, is the truest mirror of human experience. I think he's onto something.
excerpt.de: Bob Odenkirk argumentiert, dass das Formen von etwas zu 'Kunst' sich vom echten Leben entfernt — und dass Sketch-Comedy, wegwerfbar und ungeschliffen, der wahrste Spiegel menschlicher Erfahrung ist. Ich glaube, da ist etwas dran.

body.en:
Bob Odenkirk has made an argument that stuck with me: that refining and sculpting something into "art" is, in a sense, a move *away* from the human experience — and that sketch comedy, of all things, is the purest representation of it we have.

The claim sounds backwards until you sit with it. Sketch is fast, disposable, often unpolished. A bit exists, gets its laugh, and dies. There's no time to sand it into Something Important.

## Why that might make it truer

- Real life is also mostly unpolished, disposable moments — not curated monuments.
- The premium on *finish* can launder the humanity out of a thing.
- A sketch captures a specific human absurdity and then lets it go, the way life does.

## The tension worth exploring

- Is "pure" the same as "best"? Refinement clearly creates value too.
- Where's the line between craft that reveals and craft that embalms?

## Notes to self

- Find and cite the exact Odenkirk quote/source before publishing — I'm paraphrasing from memory here.
- Connect to my own work: where do I over-sculpt and lose the point?
- Keep any direct quote short and attributed; don't lean on copyrighted material.
